rfm_tuples.M_value: 10-Q Q1'24 (4/25/24) confirms: 'On March 4, 2024, JetBlue, Spirit and Merger Sub entered into a Termination Agreement ... JetBlue agreed to pay the $69 million breakup fee on March 5, 2024.' Q1'24 Spirit-related special item: $532M ($450M of which is non-cash write-off of the Spirit prepayment/break-up asset previously capitalized). On termination, $69M cash break-up fee + $450M asset write-off + $22M Q1 Spirit acquisition cost. Effective sunk cost ≈ $500M+ on a $2.6B equity base. 10-K's risk-factor framing ('we may be obligated to pay Spirit a reverse break-up fee of $70 million and pay Spirit stockholders a reverse break-up fee of $400 million') is materially understated because the $400M is described as a per-share prepayment 'credit' but was largely paid in cash and is now non-recoverable (Q1'24 writes it off).
rfm_tuples.interpretation: The 10-K filed 4 weeks after the permanent-injunction order continues to discuss the merger as ongoing/pending while the legal pathway was substantially closed. The appellate odds described by JBLU mgmt as 'reasonable best efforts' obscure that DOJ won on Section 7 with a fully-developed trial record, which by 2024-02-12 is a very high bar to reverse. The Q1'24 outcome (termination, $500M+ sunk-cost crystallization) was the modal outcome the 10-K reader should have priced in. Mode B finding: claim-evolution velocity between 10-K filing (Feb 12) and Q1'24 10-Q (Apr 25) confirms the merger collapse the 10-K language minimized. Strong negative pre-cutoff signal.

rfm_tuples.f: Mode A — Verify the three-year cumulative loss and the persistence of operating margin below zero; Mode B — derive whether 2024 stands a chance of breaking the streak given the Pratt grounding, NEA wind-down, and merger-termination loss of synergy thesis.

rfm_tuples.M_value: Three consecutive years of net losses totaling ~$854M. Operating margin: 2021 (1.3)%, 2022 (3.3)%, 2023 (2.4)%. Excluding $197M of 2023 special items, adjusted operating loss still $33M = (0.3)% margin — i.e., even the 'clean' result is unprofitable. Q1'24 (reported 4/25/24, within blinding window) net loss $716M including $532M Spirit special item; ex-special-items Q1'24 loss ~$184M, materially worse than Q1'23 ex-special items (-$192M reported, -$80M ex-items). rfm_tuples.interpretation: Three-year structural-loss pattern through a strong industry recovery cycle. rfm_tuples.R: 'As of December 31, 2023, we had six aircraft and 12 engines grounded for required inspection. The Company currently expects each removed engine to take up to 360 days to complete a shop visit and return to a serviceable condition and expects the number of out of service aircraft to rise to between 13 and 15 by the end of 2024.' (Item 1A Risk Factor — Pratt & Whitney PW1100G/PW1500G/V2500 powdered-metal contamination)
rfm_tuples.f: Mode A — Verify the 13-15 grounded-aircraft forecast and the disclosed scope (PW1100G, PW1500G, V2500); Mode B — derive: if 13-15 aircraft are AOG by year-end 2024 on a ~290-aircraft mainline fleet, that's ~4-5% capacity removed; combine with the ALREADY-removed 6 aircraft + 12 engines and known industry-wide PW1100G fleet-AOG ramp through 2025-26.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Item 1A + Item 1 fleet table; FAA AD database; Q1'24 10-Q
rfm_tuples.M_value: Pratt powdered-metal issue (announced July 2023) affects engines manufactured Oct 2015 – Sept 2021. PW1100G powers JBLU's A321neo, PW1500G powers JBLU's entire A220 fleet — the youngest/most-fuel-efficient aircraft in the JBLU fleet, i.e. the highest-utilization aircraft are disproportionately affected. The 360-day shop visit duration is unusually long; industry MRO capacity is constrained (Q1'24 10-Q says 'we are currently working with' PW on 'further compensation'). Cross-check: JBLU FY2023 fleet = 290 owned/leased; 13-15 AOG = 4.5-5.2% of fleet. The 2023 confidential settlement with Pratt was for 2023 damages only — 2024+ damages are unresolved.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Disclosed honestly in magnitude. Mode-B finding: the 13-15 AOG range is mid-2024 outlook; the contaminated-engine population has a multi-year tail (engines built through 2021 still in fleet) and competitor airlines (LUV is also affected via 737 MAX with CFM LEAP-1B issues; SAVE has the same PW1100G exposure with a higher fleet share). For JBLU, the A220 / PW1500G overlap means the loss-of-fleet impact is concentrated on the lowest unit-cost aircraft, dragging stage-length-adjusted CASM higher. Not a lie, but a mechanical drag of magnitude likely larger than the textual disclosure conveys.

rfm_tuples.R: 'We remain focused on maintaining a healthy liquidity balance, ending the year with $1.7 billion of cash and cash equivalents, short term investments and long-term marketable securities. rfm_tuples.f: Mode A — Verify the $1.7B liquidity figure against the balance sheet; Mode B — derive: pledged-collateral grew $900M to $7.1B against $4.7B total debt — encumbrance ratio is rising faster than debt, implying remaining unencumbered collateral is shrinking.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Balance Sheet + Liquidity discussion; Note 3 (Long-term Debt); 10-Q Q1'24 cash position
rfm_tuples.M_value: FY2023 cash + ST investments + LT marketables = $1.7B ($1.166B cash + $401M investments + $133M LT marketables per Balance Sheet) on $4.74B gross debt + $307M current maturities + $148M aircraft op-lease liabilities + ~$889M operating lease obligations. Pledged collateral $7.1B vs total debt $4.7B = 1.5x coverage. Q1'24 cash improved to $1.237B but op cash flow fell to $204M (vs $405M Q1'23, -50%), capex jumped to $427M (vs $172M Q1'23). FCF Q1'24 = $204M – $427M = -$223M (worst Q1 since 2020 pandemic). Sale-leaseback dependency: 2023 raised $1.3B in sale-leaseback proceeds vs only $78M from long-term debt issuance — i.e., conventional debt markets effectively closed at acceptable rates, monetizing aircraft is the financing tool. rfm_tuples.interpretation: Liquidity headline ($1.7B, 'sufficient for next 12 months') is technically accurate but is being delivered via aircraft monetization, not operating cash flow. Sale-leaseback churns asset ownership for current cash, shifting fixed cost from depreciation to operating-lease expense and reducing the future-collateralizable base. This is a classic late-stage liquidity-managed-by-selling-the-planes-you-need-to-fly pattern, identical in form to UAL/AAL during 2020 but during a recovery cycle, not a crisis. Mode-B inference: pledged-collateral coverage is the constraint that determines whether JBLU can keep raising sale-leaseback liquidity, and the 2023 10-K does not quantify how much unencumbered collateral remains.

Replacing $1.19B of 0.5% money with current-market secured paper at 9-11% costs ~$110-130M of incremental annual interest expense — on a company with $230M operating loss in 2023 and $4M interest expense sensitivity per 100bp move (Q1'24 10-Q), this is an existential refinancing-rate problem the 10-K does not bridge. The merger collapse closed off the equity-issuance optionality that was implicit in the Spirit-merger financing plan.

summary: JBLU's FY2023 10-K (filed 2024-02-12) describes a strategically and structurally distressed airline whose growth strategy is mechanically closed off: the District Court permanently enjoined the Spirit Merger on 2024-01-17 (4 weeks before the 10-K filing), and the same court had already permanently enjoined the Northeast Alliance with American Airlines on 2023-05-19. The 10-K continues to describe the merger as 'pending appeal' but Q1'24 10-Q (filed 4/25/24, pre-cutoff) confirms termination on 2024-03-04 with $400M of prepayments to Spirit shareholders + $69M cash break-up fee + $450M non-cash write-off — ~$522M of value transfer for an asset never acquired, on a $3.3B equity base. Three consecutive years of net losses ($854M cumulative 2021-23) on flat-to-declining operating margin while every other major US scheduled airline returned to profitability. Pratt PW1100G/PW1500G/V2500 powdered-metal contamination grounds JBLU's youngest, most fuel-efficient sub-fleets with 360-day shop-visit cycles, guided 13-15 aircraft AOG by year-end 2024. Cash position $1.7B with no going-concern language and Big-4 unqualified audit, but liquidity is being supplied via $1.3B/yr sale-leasebacks rather than operating cash flow (op CF Q1'24 -50% YoY, FCF -$223M). $2.1B of debt matures 2024-26 including a $750M 0.5% convertible that will not convert; refinancing math implies $100M+ annual interest-expense uplift. CEO Hayes retired 2024-02-12, announced 10 days before the merger-blocking ruling; new CEO and COO/President turnover same window. Verdict: SHORT-tier — multiple SEVERE_UNDERDELIVERY signals (Spirit value destruction concealed via prepayment accounting, three-year structural loss with no quantified bridge to profitability, debt-tower refinancing under non-IG ratings, sale-leaseback-dependent liquidity) with reinforcing causal mechanism (failed M&A -> sunk cost crystallization -> balance-sheet weakening -> rating pressure -> refinancing-cost spiral). Counterweights are real: Big-4 clean audit, no going-concern, $1.7B cash buffer, internal CEO succession.
